items.title: The Role of Color in Enhancing User Experience: A Study on Cross-Cultural Communication and Inclusive Design in Human–Computer Interaction
items.abstract: Color is a powerful visual element that transcends linguistic boundaries and communicates meaning across cultures. This study investigates color as a universal language in supporting Inclusive Design (ID), which aims to create products usable by individuals regardless of background or ability. The research examines how color influences perception, emotion, and cognition across different cultural contexts. A total of 547 design professionals from diverse disciplines were selected using stratified random sampling. Data were collected through a structured questionnaire and analyzed using SPSS software. The findings indicate that applying consistent color principles enhances cross-cultural usability and improves accessibility in design outcomes. Results also reveal that certain colors evoke similar psychological responses across countries, reinforcing their universal communicative potential. The study’s innovation lies in conceptualizing color as a shared design language that bridges cultural differences. By emphasizing strategic color decisions, this research provides practical insights for designers to create more inclusive, accessible, and culturally responsive products.

items.title: Touchscreen-Based 3D Object Manipulation: The Effects of Depth Perception Cues and Visual Feedback
items.abstract: This study investigates the efficiency of touch interaction for 3D object manipulation to enhance touchscreen user interfaces. We examined three primary tasks (move, rotate, scale) across three levels of depth perception cues (weak, moderate, strong) and visual feedback conditions (no, partial, full). Analysis of behavioral, eye-tracking, and NASA-TLX data revealed that both variables significantly impact interaction efficiency. For optimal human-machine interface (HMI) design, moderate depth perception and partial visual feedback are recommended. Additionally, visual attention strategies differ, with move and scale focusing on the entire target while rotate emphasizes local details. Cognitive load also varies, being lowest for move, moderate for rotate, and highest for scale. These findings provide a reliable theoretical and practical basis for optimizing HMI quality in interactive 3D environments.

items.title: Triadic Human–AI Collaboration in Technical Implementation for Creative Design: Cognitive Load, Team Workload, and Performance Analysis
items.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly embedded in design workflows, yet little is known about how novice designers collaborate with AI tools and human instructors. This study examined how novice design teams navigate technical implementation challenges through natural collaboration with both AI tools and instructors. Forty students in ten teams joined a four-week workshop to develop interactive installation demos. Quantitative results showed that instructor involvement increased students’ germane cognitive load, while intrinsic and extraneous cognitive load and team workload did not change significantly. Qualitative findings identified three collaboration models: co creation, task distribution, and responsibility-centered, associated with different performance levels. High performing teams and technically stronger students used AI mainly for technical support and instructors for design thinking. In contrast, medium and low performing teams and less technically skilled students relied more on both AI and instructors for problem solving and emotional support, highlighting the irreplaceable role of human instruction.

items.title: Can Business Intelligence Help Companies Avoid Compliance Troubles?
items.abstract: This study examines how the extent of business intelligence (BI) systems within business enterprises is associated with compliance risk. BI tools promote a risk-aware culture by providing real-time data and analytics, helping establish objectives aligned with compliance, and ensuring transparent communication of compliance information across the organization. Using BI, organizations can better address compliance challenges, strengthen risk management practices, and adhere to regulatory requirements more effectively. Based on a BI implementation dataset, we find that firms with more widespread BI implementation in the organization have lower compliance risk and report fewer regulatory violations and lawsuits. We also provide evidence that some measures of strategic IT focus moderate the association between BI implementation and compliance risk outcomes. Delving into the particularities of the association between BI implementation and compliance risk, we find that greater BI implementation is associated with lower lawsuit settlement amounts, fewer lawsuit types, and shorter lawsuits. Further, the beneficial association of BI implementation with compliance risk is mainly related to operational compliance risk rather than financial accounting compliance risk. Our findings have crucial implications for the value of BI in corporate compliance risk management.

items.title: Climate change and occupational health: perceptions and knowledge of heat stress in Italy
items.abstract: Context Adaptation and risk perception are key determinants in mitigating the health impacts of climate change. To guarantee compliance and enable adaptation, it is essential to raise knowledge of risks associated with heatwaves. Objectives Within the Italian “Worklimate” project, a survey was conducted in the period 2021-2022 providing the first large‑scale analysis of heat‑risk perception and knowledge among Italian workers. Methods Risk perception structure was assessed using Principal Component Analysis; group differences were examined with ANOVA and Chi-square texts, and predictors of heat risk knowledge were identified through multiple linear regression. Results The study sample consisted of 858 workers. Manual workers, along with those working outside or in settings lacking air conditioning, expressed significantly higher perceived risk compared to other groups, but not corresponding to an adequate level of actual knowledge: over 40% of respondents could not identify the signs of heatstroke or accurately implement emergency actions, and less than 30% knew that heat-related conditions can be fatal. Lack of awareness and the inadequate implementation of measures for mitigating heat stress are associated with factors such as educational level, training, and gender. Moreover, high temperatures were also widely perceived as reducing productivity. Conclusions The study highlights heat risk as an emerging priority for occupational health and safety in Italy, especially given more common and longer lasting heatwaves. The misalignment between perception and knowledge of risk implies that subjective awareness, without enough training and practical tools, is insufficient to lessen the effects of heat stress on health and productivity.

items.title: The Impact of Shift Work and Nutrition on Gastrointestinal Symptoms in Cab Drivers in England: A Mixed Methods Study
items.abstract: Background: Shift-working black cab drivers in the UK face multiple lifestyle and occupational factors that may adversely affect gastrointestinal health. Approximately 27% of UK workers engage in shift work, which is linked to irregular eating patterns, higher consumption of fatty and sugary foods, disrupted sleep cycles, and sedentary behaviour [1–7]. Cab drivers specifically experience a higher prevalence of gastrointestinal symptoms and related health risks compared to the general population, potentially due to poor dietary habits, chronic work-related stress, and limited access to nutritious food options [8–11]. Despite this, research focused on the gut health of shift-working cab drivers remains limited. Objectives: - Design and pilot a survey to capture gastrointestinal symptoms and dietary intake among licensed UK cab drivers. - Collect descriptive data on symptom severity, temporal patterns of gastrointestinal symptoms relative to shift schedules, dietary habits, and lifestyle factors including physical activity, sleep, and stress. - Explore the relationship between diet and gastrointestinal symptoms in relation to shift work. - Conduct semi-structured interviews with a purposively sampled subset to understand experiences with gastrointestinal symptoms, perceived contributing factors, coping strategies, and impacts on personal and professional life. - Identify barriers and enablers to adopting healthier dietary and lifestyle behaviours within this population. Study Design: This study uses an exploratory mixed-methods approach combining quantitative surveys and a 3-day food and symptom diary, alongside qualitative semi-structured interviews. Recruitment and Participation: The quantitative phase aims to recruit 80–110 licensed cab drivers across England through licensing authorities, taxi associations, flyers, and social media platforms. A purposive subsample of 15–20 participants will be invited for interviews until thematic saturation is reached. Participants receive shopping vouchers as incentives upon completing study phases. Data Handling and Ethics: Participant communication accommodates accessibility needs using secure WhatsApp Business on an encrypted, password-protected phone stored securely within the department when not in use. Data will be anonymised and securely stored following UK GDPR regulations. Ethical approval has been granted by King’s College London Research Ethics Committee (Ref: LRS/DP-24/25-46621). Patient and Public Involvement (PPI): Active PPI ensures the study remains relevant and ethically conducted, with involvement throughout the research process and in dissemination planning. items.title: The Triad of Excellence: A Theory Integrating Cognitive, Affective, and Psychomotor Intelligence
items.abstract: In a time where education often struggles to transcend its compartmentalized boundaries, The Triad of Excellence offers a powerful and timely solution. This groundbreaking work by Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, introduces a theory that reimagines intelligence as a fusion—an interplay between the intellectual, emotional, and physical dimensions of the human being. Rather than treating these capacities in isolation, the book proposes an integrated approach that allows them to co-elevate and reinforce one another. Drawing from decades of field experience and academic inquiry, the author creates a comprehensive vision of human potential. This is not merely a theory; it is a call for reform across educational, organizational, and developmental landscapes. By uniting the cognitive, affective, and psychomotor spheres, Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, offers a roadmap toward excellence—one rooted in synergy, purpose, and the authentic empowerment of learners and leaders alike. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, conceived this work in response to a persistent global dilemma: the fragmentation of intelligence in theory and practice. In many systems, cognitive achievement is prized while emotional understanding and embodied skill are neglected. Written in New York City and published in 1995 through UNICEF, The Triad of Excellence aims to bridge these gaps with a model grounded in human wholeness and adaptive growth. At the core of this book lies a refined definition of intelligence—not as an isolated trait, but as a triadic process composed of cognitive clarity, emotional resonance, and physical execution. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, articulates that excellence is not attained through intellect alone but through the synchronization of thought, feeling, and movement. This integrated intelligence model challenges existing academic silos and proposes a complete developmental framework. The need for this theory emerged from consistent global patterns: students with high IQs yet lacking empathy, professionals with emotional depth but limited critical reasoning, and athletes or performers with physical mastery but insufficient self-awareness. These recurring contradictions inspired Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, to search for a deeper alignment of human faculties and to create a theory that reflects this synthesis. The Triad of Excellence is anchored in key principles: mutual enhancement among faculties, self-directed growth through feedback, environmental adaptability, and holistic assessment. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, emphasizes learning that is meaningful, embodied, and emotionally rich, with continuous calibration between internal capacities and external demands. Growth in this model is marked by indicators that extend beyond test scores or performance reviews. These include the learner’s ability to synthesize ideas, respond to emotional cues, maintain focus under pressure, and translate insight into action. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, proposes dynamic tools for tracking such growth over time. The theory rests upon operational variables such as neurobiological readiness, emotional stability, cognitive engagement, cultural framing, and motor skill responsiveness. Each is examined in its relational influence on the triad, with practical strategies for enhancement. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, unpacks how these can be observed and supported in learning environments. Key determinants of success within this framework include educator sensitivity, systemic flexibility, learner agency, and societal narratives surrounding intelligence. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, presents these as crucial factors that either foster or inhibit excellence, depending on their alignment with the triadic model. Implementation requires an adaptive strategy, one that invites collaboration across domains. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, provides blueprints for educational institutions, leadership programs, and youth development centers to adopt this theory. He emphasizes inclusive curriculum design, emotional coaching, and movement-based learning experiences. While promising, the theory faces challenges such as institutional rigidity, teacher burnout, and socio-cultural resistance. Yet, enabling dynamics—such as policy reform, digital platforms, and interdisciplinary research—offer avenues for support. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, candidly explores both forces and suggests ways to navigate them. Ultimately, The Triad of Excellence leaves us with a profound realization: true intelligence is not fragmented, but integrated. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, offers not just a framework but a future vision, where learners are empowered to become balanced, resilient, and whole. His synthesis is not only theoretical—it is a blueprint for evolving human capacity in every sphere of life. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) is an Indonesian scholar, academic leader, and social development advocate with a strong multidisciplinary background. In 2016, YER was awarded the title of Doctor of Humanity, holds a Ph.D. in Information Technology and a DBA in Technology Management. Since 2016, YER has been actively teaching and collaborating with international universities in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and the United States. YER is the founder of the Education Training Centre (ETC, 1992), YER Academic Publishing (YERA, 1993), the Multidisciplinary Academic Institute of Learning (MAIL, 1998), and YER E-Book Publishing (YERE, 1999), institutions dedicated to education, interdisciplinary learning, and ethical academic publishing. His academic contributions have led to his recognition as a Professor and his affiliation with the World Philosophy Foundation. YER is also actively involved in global development initiatives through the United Nations, as a member of the UN Global Compact (id-137635), the UN Global Market (id-709131), and the UN ECOSOC (id-677556). YER has served as a reviewer for several international journals and book chapters, and has written numerous books and articles on a wide range of topics including Philosophy, Economics, Management, items.title: AI-Enhanced Modular Material Selection for Patient-Specific Diabetic Insoles via Silicone Molding
items.abstract: ObjectiveThis study proposes an AI-enhanced modular material selection approach for designing diabetic insoles. By customizing materials for forefoot and heel modules, the method enables personalized support and pressure redistribution, resulting in cost-effective insoles.BackgroundDiabetic foot ulcers occur as a result of elevated plantar pressure and poor foot sensation. To mitigate this risk, developing insoles that redistribute plantar pressure can significantly lower the likelihood of ulcer formation.MethodThe insole was fabricated using cost-effective silicone molding, with functional personalization achieved via an AI-enhanced approach that selected optimal, interchangeable cushioning materials for forefoot and heel modules of each patient. The design integrates a ¾-length porous silicone upper layer with regionally optimized materials. Laboratory wear trials involving 23 diabetic patients compared the offloading performance of the hybrid insole (AIO) against barefoot, a PORON® Medical 4708 insole (PUR), and a cork-EVA insole (EVA).ResultsAIO demonstrated a 37.6% reduction in peak plantar pressure compared to barefoot condition while increasing contact area by 36.0% across the plantar surface. It significantly outperformed the commercial insole (EVA) and matched a therapeutic insole (PUR) overall, with superior regional offloading at the heel.ConclusionThis study enhances diabetic foot care by combining efficiency of silicone molding with functionally personalized, modular design to achieve superior pressure redistribution. It establishes a paradigm of "modular personalization" for diabetic insoles, leveraging AI for patient-specific material selection within a standardized, biomechanically optimized geometry.ApplicationThe findings offer practical insights for clinicians and manufacturers seeking scalable, patient-specific solutions for preventing diabetic foot ulcers.

items.title: AI, autism, and the architecture of voice: from engineered exclusion to designed dignity
items.abstract: Abstract This paper conceptualizes engineered exclusion —the predictable sidelining of disabled users resulting from choices about data provenance, model objectives, and evaluation practices within AI systems. We examine engineered exclusion through the lived experiences of minimally and nonspeaking autistic people whose communicative profiles challenge the speech-centered defaults embedded in contemporary AI pipelines. Here, “voice” refers not only to speech but to the broader architecture through which embodied, multimodal communication—spanning AAC text, gesture, movement, and partial vocalizations—becomes legible within AI systems. “Nonspeaking” is therefore not the absence of language but a heterogeneous spectrum in which communication is often state dependent, varying with fatigue, anxiety, sensory load, and motor planning demands—forms of variation that design abstractions routinely erase. Tracing exclusionary mechanisms across speech recognition, text-to-speech, plain-language systems, and interface design, we introduce measurable designed-dignity metrics for technical evaluation (Table 1) and a governance framework mapping accountability across the AI lifecycle (Table 2). We argue that accessibility must be treated as a core dimension of AI ethics—on par with fairness, privacy, and safety. Re-engineering AI for designed dignity requires systems that recognize embodied, multimodal, and fluctuating forms of communication, expanding what counts as valid signal and responsible innovation.

items.title: Between humans and algorithms: framing machine communication as a socio-technical relation
items.abstract: Abstract This theoretical essay proposes an integrative framework for analyzing machine speech, the autonomous generation of linguistically interpretable content by computational systems that acquires institutional legitimation and carries decision-bearing weight in social, organizational, and communicational contexts. The framework is built around three foundational traditions: Norbert Wiener’s cybernetics, Marshall McLuhan’s media theory, and Marvin Minsky’s society of mind. Rather than treating these traditions sequentially, the essay reads them together across three constitutive dimensions of the problem while mobilizing Latour’s actor-network theory as the relational ontology that connects agency, materiality, and accountability across all three dimensions. From this integrated reading, the essay derives and operationalizes a diagnostic triad of modalities through which machine speech operates, complementarity, substitution and coconstruction. The triad is advanced not as a taxonomy of AI systems but as an analytical instrument for identifying how communicational agency, visibility, and accountability are configured differently across these three modes. Each modality implies a distinct accountability regime. The essay argues that theorizing machine communication requires moving beyond transmission models toward a relational understanding of agency as a sociotechnical achievement distributed across humans, algorithms, data, and infrastructures.

items.title: Designing Sustainable workplaces: the strategic role of ergonomics and employee well-being
items.abstract: Workplace social sustainability supports employee satisfaction, health, and organisational goals; however, the specific contribution of Human Factors and Ergonomics (HFE) to Sustainable Development Goal 3 (SDG 3: Good Health and Well-Being) at the individual workplace level remains underexplored. This study integrates Decision-Making Trial and Evaluation Laboratory (DEMATEL) and Analytic Network Process (ANP) as network-based Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) approaches capable of modelling interdependencies among criteria to identify and prioritise determinants of workplace social sustainability. Twenty industry experts assessed 17 validated indicators spanning five core dimensions. Results indicate that employee well-being is the most critical driver of workplace social sustainability, while musculoskeletal health is less influential. The DEMATEL-ANP hybrid approach clarified cause-effect structures and derived relative importance weights across all criteria, providing actionable insights for embedding social sustainability into organisational policies and supporting targeted interventions that advance SDG 3 in workplace contexts.

items.title: Differences in upper limb load between sitting and standing postures: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.abstract: The aim of the study was to quantify the differences in upper limb loads between standing and sitting postures. Workstations that secure alterations between sitting and standing are a novel occupational intervention. Knowing the differences in upper limb musculoskeletal load between sitting and standing would allow for a more complex assessment of work-related exposure and establishing the optimal timing of transitions between sitting and standing. The data from the literature search (upper limb muscles strength and activity recorded while sitting and standing) were analyzed using a continuous random effects model. Pooling was conducted using the Ratio of Means with inverse variance weighting. Egger's regression test, along with Duval and Tweedie's trim and fill approach assessed and corrected publication bias. The Cochran's Q, Tau 2 , and I 2 evaluated heterogeneity. The results revealed increased muscular activity while sitting. The deltoid muscle had the largest effect size, the trapezius a somewhat smaller. The biceps and triceps muscles produced a low effect size. Wrist extensor exhibited the opposite tendency. In the case of forces (handgrip and pulling), a small effect size indicates more force capabilities in standing. Concluding - in a standing posture the contraction of the upper limb muscles is lower than when performing the same tasks during sitting. Impact of posture on upper limb maximum strength capabilities is inconclusive. The results can give input to establishing optimal time of alterations between sitting and standing and to development of methods that serve to assessment of work-related upper limbs exposure.

items.title: Motivated Reading: Eye Movements Reveal Low-Level Avoidance of Attitude-Incongruent Information
items.abstract: People tend to seek and engage with information that aligns with their pre-existing beliefs rather than challenges them, reinforcing ideological echo chambers and polarization. While prior research has focused on high-level choices (e.g., what people want to read and how they evaluate it), the present study asks whether motivated cognition manifests at the fundamental level of reading. Using eye-tracking, we monitored participants (N=76) - half vegetarian and half non-vegetarian - each reading short factual paragraphs about the positive and negative implications of vegetarianism, resulting in a total of 756 trials (i.e., reads of passages). Consistent with our hypothesis, there was a significant interaction between participants’ stance and the text’s argument on reading behavior: Readers skipped more words when texts opposed rather than aligned with their stance, indicating reduced cognitive engagement with attitude-incongruent content. This attitude-congruency effect emerged in both overall and first-run skipping measures. This research reveals that existing beliefs don’t just dictate what we read, they change how we read. By reducing engagement with incongruent content, this selective skimming acts as an underlying mechanism that creates a cognitive barrier, preventing new information from being fully processed. These findings suggest that motivated cognition operates already during early information intake, revealing a mechanism through which worldview-consistent biases take root.

items.title: Socio-technical models for AI-driven enterprise operations: a systematic literature review of integration gaps in observability, human factors, and economic evaluation under emerging economy constraints
items.abstract: This systematic literature review examines the state of the art in socio-technical models applied to AI-driven enterprise operations. The title reflects four interconnected conceptual decisions that define the scope and contribution of the review. The term "socio-technical models" positions the review within the tradition of systems theory that recognizes the interdependence of social and technical dimensions in organizational contexts (Trist & Bamforth, 1951; Emery & Trist, 1969). Rather than examining technology in isolation, the review focuses on frameworks that jointly address processes, people, and technology as structurally integrated components. The phrase "AI-driven enterprise operations" delimits the application domain to organizational settings where artificial intelligence acts as an enabler of operational processes, including but not limited to automation, intelligent decision support, AIOps, MLOps, and AI-augmented business process management. This distinguishes the review from studies that treat AI as a purely technical object of study, and from organizational studies that address digital transformation without specific focus on AI as an operational enabler. The phrase "integration gaps" signals the analytical orientation of the review. Rather than cataloguing existing models descriptively, the review is designed to identify structural absences: dimensions that existing models fail to incorporate in an integrated manner. Three integration gaps are foregrounded in the title and constitute the primary analytical lens of the review. The first gap concerns "observability": the extent to which existing models connect technical monitoring and operational visibility with organizational value-generation decisions, rather than treating observability as a purely technical practice disconnected from business outcomes. The second gap concerns "human factors": the extent to which existing models incorporate the human dimension as a structural axis of design rather than as a moderating variable or implementation afterthought. This includes resistance to change, organizational culture, adoption readiness, and the development of human capabilities as conditions for sustained value generation. The third gap concerns "economic evaluation": the extent to which existing models integrate explicit economic criteria such as Return on Investment (ROI) and Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) as components of the model itself, rather than as external metrics applied post hoc. Finally, the qualifier "emerging economy constraints" signals a contextual boundary condition that distinguishes this review from prior work. The majority of validated socio-technical models have been developed and tested in high-income economies with well-developed digital infrastructure, established organizational maturity, and stable investment capacity. Emerging economies, and Latin America in particular, present a distinct combination of economic restrictions, short-term organizational orientation, digital infrastructure gaps, and cultural factors that limit the direct transferability of existing models. The review examines whether and how this contextual specificity has been addressed in the literature, and identifies it as a structural gap requiring dedicated theoretical and empirical attention. Together, these four conceptual decisions define a review that is not a general survey of socio-technical systems literature, but a theoretically motivated and practically oriented analysis of a specific set of integration failures in a specific application domain and context. The expected contribution is a structured map of what exists, what is missing, and what type of integrated model would be needed to close the identified gaps — providing the theoretical foundation for subsequent model design and empirical validation. items.title: A method based on double-weighted closeness centrality for identifying firefighting strategies in industrial plants considering domino effects
items.abstract: • Domino effects are modeled as double-weighted directed graphs. • New relationships are developed for ‘distance’ and ‘closeness centrality’ • Firefighting strategies are identified by minimizing the closeness of burning units. • The method is easy to implement as it is independent of fire spread probabilities. Firefighting at process plants is considered the last line of defence in fire protection. As such, the success and efficiency of firefighting strategies directly impact the safety, integrity, and damage cost of process plants and adjacent on-site and off-site structures and facilities. Suppressing burning units while cooling exposed units is the most intuitive strategy, which is also practiced at process plants, for preventing fire spread and potential domino effects, assuming that firefighting resources (equipment, crew, water, etc.) are sufficient to deal with all the burning and exposed units. However, when firefighting resources are insufficient, models are required to help firefighters identify the most critical units and prioritize viable firefighting strategies accordingly. In the present study, after modelling domino effects as a double-weighted directed graph, i.e., a graph with weighted nodes and edges, it is shown that effective firefighting strategies can be identified by minimizing the closeness centrality of burning units. The developed method not only results in consistent firefighting strategies compared with the risk-based methods in the literature, but also requires fewer input parameters (basically, heat flux and asset monetary values), alleviating the need for calculating the fire escalation probabilities.

items.title: Appearance-free Action Recognition: Zero-shot Generalization in Humans and a Two-Pathway Model
items.abstract: Action recognition is a fundamental ability for social species. Yet, its underlying computations are not well understood. Classical psychophysical studies using simplified stimuli have shown that humans can perceive body motion even under degradation of relevant shape cues. Recent work using real-world action videos and their appearance-free counterparts (that preserve motion but lack static shape cues) included explicit training of humans and models on the appearance-free videos. Whether humans and vision models generalize in a zero-shot manner to appearance-free transformations of real-world action videos is not yet known. To measure this generalization in humans, we conducted a laboratory-based psychophysics experiment. 22 participants were trained to recognize five action categories using naturalistic videos (UCF5 dataset), and tested zero-shot on two types of appearance-free transformations: (i) dense-noise motion videos from an existing dataset (AFD5) and (ii) random-dot appearance-free videos. We find that participants recognize actions in both types of appearance-free videos well above chance, albeit with reduced accuracy compared to naturalistic videos. To model this behavior, we developed a two-pathway 3D CNN-based model combining an RGB (form) stream and an optical flow (motion) stream, including a coherence-gating mechanism inspired by Gestalt common-fate grouping. Our model generalizes to both appearance-free datasets and outperforms contemporary video classification models, narrowing the gap to human performance. We find that the motion pathway is critical for generalization to appearance-free videos, while the form pathway improves performance on naturalistic videos. Our findings highlight the importance of motion-based representations for generalization to appearance-free videos, and support the use of multi-stream architectures to model video-based action recognition.

items.title: Artificial Effort
items.abstract: Real-effort tasks, in which participants perform cognitively costly activities whose outcomes depend on actual performance, are widely used in experimental economics. Their validity, however, rests on the assumption that a human performs them. We study whether this assumption still holds in the era of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Large Language Models (LLMs). Using 8 canonical real-effort tasks and 23 LLMs from three major providers, we show that most tasks can now be solved accurately and at a negligible cost, while only a few resist automation. Performance improves with each model generation, and midtier models are rapidly closing the gap with frontier ones, broadening the set of widely accessible models that can automate these tasks. Additionally, we show that verbally offering monetary incentives has no effect on LLM performance. Our findings establish a boundary condition for the use of real-effort tasks in unsupervised settings: when participants can cheaply outsource task completion to an LLM, observed performance may no longer reflect genuine human effort.

items.title: Beyond Algorithm Aversion: The Role of Power Relationships in Shaping Mutual Trust in Human-AI Team
items.abstract: In the era of artificial intelligence, users’ attitudes toward algorithms play a critical role in shaping trust and acceptance of AI technologies. However, previous research has overlooked dispositional trust toward algorithms and its role in shaping bidrectional trust in human-AI interaction. To address these gaps, this paper introduces the concept of algorithm aversion tendency (AAT) and develops the AAT scale to capture users’ general trust attitudes towards algorithms. It further examines the cognitive pathways through AAT influences bidirectional trust and behavior intention. The results indicate that AAT has a significant negative effect on trust in AI and behavior intention. The effect remains significant across different human-AI power relationships. However, the effect of AAT on trust is moderated by power relationships. Overall, this study highlights the critical role of dispositional trust in algorithms in shaping trust and behavioral intention in human–AI interaction.

items.title: Designing More Engaging Serious Games to Support Students' Mental Health: A Pilot Study Based on A CBT-Informed Design Framework
items.abstract: Addressing the issues of dullness, low compliance, and lack of appeal in current digital mental health education and serious games for students and adolescents, this study proposes a novel, experience-centered framework for serious game design: the Therapeutic Procedural Rhetoric and Mechanism Mapping Framework (TPR-MMF). Based on this framework, a side-scrolling serious game prototype, "World + You - World," was developed. This study compared the effectiveness of TPR-MMF-based games with traditional explicit educational serious games through a small-sample randomized controlled trial (N=28). The results of the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (IMI) showed that the experimental group (playing "World + You - World") significantly outperformed the control group in four aspects. Furthermore, qualitative survey results indicated that players could perceive the psychological metaphors within the game mechanics and spontaneously resonated with real-life experiences. This study provides a highly engaging new development paradigm for gamified mental health education for students and adolescents.

items.title: Digital Platforms and Collaborative Consumption: Examining User Attitudes and Behavioral Intentions in Food Delivery Services
items.abstract: Digital food delivery platforms are reshaping real-time consumer decision-making, yet the interactive effects of platform features remain underexplored. Drawing on the Theory of Planned Behavior, this study examines Google’s micro-moment strategies—Be There, Be Useful, and Be Accountable—as an tecedents of attitudes, perceived behavioral control, and behavioral intentions in collaborative consumption contexts. A 2 × 2 × 2 factorial experiment was conducted with 260 dyads (N = 520 individuals), with dyads as the unit of analysis. Results revealed a significant three-way interaction: timely, relevant, and trustworthy information produced the strongest attitudinal evaluations. Structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) and Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) results supported most hypothesized relationships. The findings extend the TPB to collaborative digital consumption, demonstrating that platform features operate synergistically rather than independently, and offer practical implications for food-delivery interface design and real-time decision support systems..

items.title: Electronic Records Management Systems: A Literature Review
items.abstract: The increasing reliance on digital infrastructures has made electronic records management systems (ERMS) essential for ensuring organisational governance, accountability, and effective service delivery. This study presents a structured qualitative literature review of ERMS implementation across developed and developing contexts, with the aim of identifying key determinants, recurring challenges, and contextual variations in adoption patterns. Drawing on studies published between 2010 and 2024, the review adopts a socio-technical analytical framework that categorises ERMS implementation determinants into organisational, technological, and environmental dimensions. The findings reveal that successful implementation depends on the alignment of governance and policy frameworks (environmental), technological infrastructure and system capabilities (technological), and human resource capacity and organisational culture (organisational). The analysis further demonstrates that these determinants are highly interdependent and vary across contexts. In developing environments, implementation is primarily constrained by infrastructural limitations, financial constraints, and shortages of technical expertise. In contrast, in more digitally mature contexts, challenges shift toward system interoperability, usability, and metadata standardisation. This study contributes to the literature by providing an integrated analytical framework that synthesises fragmented empirical findings and advances a more structured understanding of ERMS implementation as a sociotechnical process. The findings offer practical implications for policymakers and institutions seeking to strengthen digital records management and information governance. Future research should prioritise longitudinal and cross-national studies to further advance theoretical development in this field.

items.title: Human Cognition in Machines: A Unified Perspective of World Models
items.abstract: This report of world models distinguishes prior works by the cognitive functions they innovate. Many works claim an almost human-like cognitive capability in their world models. To evaluate these claims requires a proper grounding in first principles from human and machine cognition theory. In moving towards human-like world models we present a conceptual unified framework for world models that fully incorporates all the cognitive functions (i.e., memory, perception, language, reasoning, imagining, motivation, and metacognition) and identify gaps in existing research as a guide for future states of the art. In particular, we find that motivation (especially intrinsic motivation) and metacognition remain drastically under-researched, and we propose concrete directions to address these gaps informed by active inference and global workspace theory. We also introduce epistemic world models, a new category encompassing agent frameworks for scientific discovery that operate over structured knowledge. Our taxonomy, applied to video, embodied, and epistemic world models, suggests research directions where prior taxonomies have not.

items.title: Managing the ethical risks of AI in intelligence: a multi-layered framework
items.abstract: Abstract This article develops a context-sensitive multi-level harm–threat ethical framework for assessing the permissibility of artificial intelligence (AI) in intelligence operations, with particular focus on harms to privacy and autonomy. AI offers unprecedented capabilities in data collection, analysis, and predictive modeling, enabling more efficient and effective detection and prevention of threats. At the same time, its use in intelligence contexts intensifies the scale, depth, and persistence of intrusions, while reshaping how intelligence operatives understand their roles, judgements, and reliance on algorithmically generated information. The ethical challenge, therefore, is not whether intelligence-AI causes harm, but how such harm can be morally assessed, constrained, and justified throughout the process. This paper addresses this challenge by developing a multi-level harm–threat framework that evaluates ethical permissibility by systematically linking the degree of harm imposed to the severity, proximity, evidentiary strength, and target liability of the anticipated threat. Embedded within the intelligence cycle, the framework captures how AI-driven collection, processing, analysis, and implementation progressively intensify intrusion through profiling and prediction. The paper’s contribution lies in translating normative ethical reasoning into an operational justificatory logic that guides intelligence decision-making without normalizing ambient or disproportionate surveillance.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: Motivational Profiles and Interaction Patterns in Cultural Heritage Virtual Reality: A Latent Profile Analysis Grounded in Self-Determination Theory
items.abstract: Virtual Reality (VR) is increasingly used to support cultural heritage experiences, yet most studies still focus on technology and storytelling, paying relatively little attention to how different types of motivation relate to users’ interactive behaviors. Drawing on Self-Determination Theory (SDT) and Organismic Integration Theory (OIT), this study identifies latent motivational types among Cultural Heritage Virtual Reality (CH-VR) users and examines their antecedents and interaction patterns. Using Latent Profile Analysis (LPA) on survey data from 544 users, it reveals five user types differing in autonomy: autonomously driven, externally controlled, mixed-motivation, responsibility-identified, and amotivated. The results indicate that users’ levels of cultural knowledge and cultural identity significantly predict profile membership. Moreover, autonomously driven users exhibit higher levels of participatory interaction, cognitive interaction, perceptual interaction and social interaction than externally controlled and amotivated users. These findings extend the application of self-determination theory to VR-based cultural heritage contexts and inform the design of personalized CH-VR experiences.

items.title: Reckoning with the Political Economy of AI: Avoiding Decoys in Pursuit of Accountability
items.abstract: The Project of AI is a world-building endeavor, wherein those who fund and develop AI systems both operate through and seek to sustain networks of power and wealth. As they expand their access to resources and configure our sociotechnical conditions, they benefit from the ways in which a suite of decoys animate scholars, critics, policymakers, journalists, and the public into co-constructing industry-empowering AI futures. Regardless of who constructs or nurtures them, these decoys often create the illusion of accountability while both masking the emerging political economies that the Project of AI has set into motion, and also contributing to the network-making power that is at the heart of the Project's extraction and exploitation. Drawing on literature at the intersection of communication, science and technology studies, and economic sociology, we examine how the Project of AI is constructed. We then explore five decoys that seemingly critique - but in actuality co-constitute - AI's emergent power relations and material political economy. We argue that advancing meaningful fairness or accountability in AI requires: 1) recognizing when and how decoys serve as a distraction, and 2) grappling directly with the material political economy of the Project of AI. Doing so will enable us to attend to the networks of power that make 'AI' possible, spurring new visions for how to realize a more just technologically entangled world.

items.title: The Impact of Internet Use on Happiness—An Analysis from the Perspective of Work-Life Boundary
items.abstract: Information technology is becoming more recognized by researchers as a major tool for improving well-being. Using data from the 2020 and 2022 China Family Panel Studies, this study examines the impact of internet use on happiness from the perspective of work-life boundaries. The findings of this study are as follows: (1) There is a significant positive correlation between internet use and the blurring of the work-life boundaries. (2) The blurring of the work-life boundary plays a negative mediating role between internet use and happiness. (3) Work flexibility further reinforces the role of the blurring of the work-life boundary in the relationship between internet use and happiness. This study contributes to the research on the relationship between internet use and well-being and provides evidence for understanding the impact of information technology on people's work-life boundaries.

items.title: A Study on Human Performance Prediction Method in a Main Control Room of Nuclear Power Plants
items.abstract: Human performance exerts a significant influence on the safety of nuclear power plants (NPPs). However, due to its inherent dynamism and the paucity of relevant data, developing an effective method for predicting human performance remains a pressing challenge. To address this issue, this study takes the main control room (MCR) of NPPs as its research context and proposes an intelligent prediction method for human performance. Specifically, a hybrid architectural approach integrating backpropagation (BP) and radial basis function neural networks is developed. The primary framework employs a BP network structure, with the input layer utilizing a Gaussian basis function to preprocess input data. Sample data were derived from 17 operational scenarios at an NPP in China. Training results indicate that the proposed method exhibits favorable predictive performance, with errors within an acceptable range. This approach thus enables dynamic, timely, and effective prediction of human performance in NPPs.

items.title: AI-powered smartphone tools and immigrant social integration. The role of personality and psychological factors
items.abstract: This study investigates the potential of AI-powered mobile applications (m-Integration) to enhance the integration process for immigrants. Leveraging Sen’s capability approach framework and self-determination theory, we explore how the adoption and effectiveness of these applications are influenced by individual factors such as personality traits, self-esteem, resilience, and emotional intelligence. Using quantitative survey data collected from 748 immigrants in Finland—particularly those attending free language classes across five major cities—we examine how AI-driven tools support societal integration in a country facing workforce shortages due to an aging population and an influx of immigrants from conflict zones such as Ukraine and Russia. By employing ordinary least squares (OLS) regression models, we analyze the determinants of AI-powered application use and its impact on integration outcomes measured by the Ethnosizer index. The findings reveal that AI-powered applications facilitate smoother and more efficient integration processes, with attitudes toward these technologies strongly linked to personality and psychological profiles. Immigrants exhibiting high levels of openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, resilience, self-esteem, and emotional intelligence are more likely to adopt and benefit from these tools. This study provides novel insights into the intersection of AI technology and immigrant integration, offering policy-makers evidence-based strategies to leverage AI to promote social inclusion and address integration challenges in diverse populations. • AI mobile apps aid immigrant integration via resilience and emotional intelligence. • M-Integration adoption relates to openness, conscientiousness, and extraversion. • AI tools ease integration; attitudes shaped by self-esteem and emotions. • Offers insights for policymakers to harness AI for social inclusion.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Chatbots as Relational Agents: A Systematic Review of Human–AI Chatbot Relationships
items.abstract: This study presents a systematic review guided by the human–AI chatbot Relationship (HAIR) Framework of Social Influence to clarify the antecedents of human–AI chatbot relationships and their social influence outcomes. Following PRISMA guidelines, we searched six databases (ACM Digital Library, Web of Science, Scopus, IEEE, EBSCO, and PsycINFO) and identified 16,358 records, of which 68 papers (78 studies) met inclusion criteria. Findings reveal that trust and perceived social support frequently functioned as relational mediators through which chatbots exert social influence. Although chatbot design features were most commonly examined, message-level factors such as empathy and responsiveness showed extensive associations with relational outcomes but remain underexplored. The literature is dominated by short-term experimental designs, inconsistent conceptualizations of key constructs, and Western samples, limiting understanding of long-term and cross-cultural relationship development. This study clarifies the relational processes underlying AI chatbot influence and offers directions for designing more effective human–AI communication.

items.title: Bureaucratic Silences: What the Canadian AI Register Reveals, Omits, and Obscures
items.abstract: In November 2025, the Government of Canada operationalized its commitment to transparency by releasing its first Federal AI Register. In this paper, we argue that such registers are not neutral mirrors of government activity, but active instruments of ontological design that configure the boundaries of accountability. We analyzed the Register's complete dataset of 409 systems using the Algorithmic Decision-Making Adapted for the Public Sector (ADMAPS) framework, combining quantitative mapping with deductive qualitative coding. Our findings reveal a sharp divergence between the rhetoric of "sovereign AI" and the reality of bureaucratic practice: while 86\% of systems are deployed internally for efficiency, the Register systematically obscures the human discretion, training, and uncertainty management required to operate them. By privileging technical descriptions over sociotechnical context, the Register constructs an ontology of AI as "reliable tooling" rather than "contestable decision-making." We conclude that without a shift in design, such transparency artifacts risk automating accountability into a performative compliance exercise, offering visibility without contestability.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: CogEvolution: A Human-like Generative Educational Agent to Simulate Student's Cognitive Evolution
items.abstract: Generative Agents, owing to their precise modeling and simulation capabilities of human behavior, have become a pivotal tool in the field of Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIEd) for uncovering complex cognitive processes of learners. However, existing educational agents predominantly rely on static personas to simulate student learning behaviors, neglecting the decisive role of deep cognitive capabilities in learning outcomes during practice interactions. Furthermore, they struggle to characterize the dynamic fluidity of knowledge internalization, transfer, and cognitive state transitions. To overcome this bottleneck, this paper proposes a human-like educational agent capable of simulating student cognitive evolution: CogEvolution. Specifically, we first construct a cognitive depth perceptron based on the Interactive, Constructive, Active, Passive (ICAP) taxonomy from cognitive psychology, achieving precise quantification of learner cognitive engagement. Subsequently, we propose a memory retrieval method based on Item Response Theory (IRT) to simulate the connection and assimilation of new and prior knowledge. Finally, we design a dynamic cognitive update mechanism based on evolutionary algorithms to simulate the real-time integration of student learning behaviors and cognitive evolution processes. Comprehensive evaluations demonstrate that CogEvolution not only significantly outperforms baseline models in behavioral fidelity and learning curve fitting but also uniquely reproduces plausible and robust cognitive evolutionary paths consistent with educational psychology expectations, providing a novel paradigm for constructing highly interpretable educational agents.

items.title: Cyber-Physical Technologies and Perception Intelligence: A New Approach to International Media Communication
items.abstract: The emergence of cognitive intelligence, which is a combination of artificial intelligence (AI), the Internet of Things (IoT), and cognitive computing, has altered the culture of communication in movies and television shows around the world. This study addresses how perception intelligence (PI) could be employed as a tool of international cross-cultural communication through film and television (FTV). Mixed-methods approach was employed. The quantitative data were gathered from 643 professionals working with PI in the FTV industry using an online survey. The qualitative information were gathered using follow-up interviews with 120 participants. It was found that PI greatly improves international cultural communication (CC) with the delivery of adaptive content and the possibility to interact with audience using the IoT and enhanced visual experiences based on cyber-physical technologies (CPT). This study is novel as it proposes an integrated cyber-physical and cognitive-intelligence framework for FTV.

items.title: Differential Game With Motor Intent Prediction for Diverging Human Motion Plan
items.abstract: When a human controls a robot directly or via teleoperation, incomplete information and unpredictable environmental conditions can lead to conflicts between their plans. Differential game theory (GT) offers a framework for optimal robotic assistance, but existing methods for identifying the human model require a shared plan. This article introduces an approach to deal with a diverging human plan by leveraging a neuromechanical model of their viscoelasticity to directly estimate their motion intent during movement. The viscoelastic gains can then be integrated into a GT framework to compute optimal contribution of the robot to the common motor task. We evaluated the proposed method in experiments, comparing it with fixed impedance control and nonoptimal variable impedance control. Results demonstrate stable interactions even in the presence of conflicting motion plans, and superior performance relative to these two alternative methods.

items.title: Driver's Perceived Risk Prediction Method Based on Semisupervised Learning Strategy
items.abstract: Safety has become a critical issue in the development of automated driving systems (ADSs). Drivers' perception of risk determines their acceptance, trust, and use of ADS. However, driver's perceived risk is subjective and difficult to evaluate using traditional risk assessment methods. To address this issue, a driver's subjective perceived risk (DSPR) model is proposed, which regards driver's perceived risk as a dynamically triggered mechanism that exhibits anisotropy and attenuation. Subsequently, 20 participants are recruited for a driver-in-the-loop experiment to report their real-time subjective risk ratings (SRRs) when experiencing various real-world automated driving scenarios. A convolutional neural network and bidirectional long short-term memory with temporal pattern attention (CNN-Bi-LSTM-TPA) network is embedded into a semisupervised learning strategy to predict driver's SRRs, aiming to reduce data noise caused by the subjective randomness of drivers. Results illustrate that our proposed DSPR model combined with the semisupervised learning strategy achieves the highest prediction accuracy of 87.91% in predicting driver's SRRs, outperforming other three state-of-the-art risk models. Compared to the model trained on the original data, the semisupervised method improves accuracy by 20.12%. The proposed CNN-Bi-LSTM-TPA network presents the highest among four different network structures. Finally, a genetic algorithm is applied to optimize parameters, which improves the accuracy to 89.95%. This study offers an effective method for assessing driver's perceived risk, providing support for the safety enhancement of ADS and driver's trust improvement.

items.title: Empirical Comparison of K-Means Initialization Methods for Card Sorting Data Analysis
items.abstract: Card sorting is a user research method used to gain insights into how people categorize and comprehend information. Analysis of the collected data typically involves using clustering algorithms, such as the K-means algorithm. However, it is well established that the efficiency and accuracy of the K-means is greatly affected by the initialization method used. This paper empirically compares seven K-means initialization methods for analyzing card sorting datasets using six metrics of clustering quality. We used a card sorting dataset from a real-world study for redesigning the information architecture of a University e-learning platform, involving 112 participants and 50 cards. It was found that the Best Merge Method provides the best results when analyzing open card sort datasets from 30 or fewer participants. When the number of participants exceeds 30, the Best Merge Method and Actual Agreement Method are the most effective approaches to employ.

items.title: Eye-Tracking in Statistical Graphics Research: A Scoping Review
items.abstract: Quantitative data analysis increasingly relies on statistical graphics, necessitating a deeper understanding of their effectiveness. Eye-tracking is a valuable tool for exploring how users interact with these visualizations. However, despite several systematic reviews of the fields of statistical visualizations and the application of eye-tracking technology, a review specifically focusing on eye-tracking in statistical graphics research has been lacking. This article addresses this gap with a systematic PRISMA-based scoping review of 114 empirical studies, critically examining their methodologies, key findings, and implications. We conclude that while eye-tracking offers profound insights, improved methodological practices, including more robust experimental designs, appropriate statistical modeling, and broader participant sampling, are essential to unlock its full potential in advancing our understanding of statistical graphics.
